title: The hen on her eggs
hookLine: Ananda: keep practice warm like a hen on her eggs, and the chicks break out

cards: The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, the Buddha's own people, have built a brand-new assembly hall. Nobody has used it yet. They ask the Buddha to be the first, to bless it with a teaching.
He comes, and teaches late into the night. Then his back begins to ache. So he asks Ananda to go on teaching, and lies down on his right side, mindful, to rest.
Ananda, with the Buddha listening, takes the floor.

teach.b: This is the fifty-third discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, on the disciple in training. Ananda speaks to Mahanama, a Sakyan noble, about someone who isn't finished yet but is on the way.
They keep the precepts and guard the senses. They eat in moderation and stay wakeful for practice. They have faith, conscience, care, learning, energy, mindfulness and wisdom.
And they can reach the four deep absorptions when they wish. Then Ananda gives a picture from any farmyard.

teach.h: A HEN SITS ON HER EGGS
teach.b: A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. She sits on them properly, keeps them warm, broods them well.

teach.h: THE CHICKS BREAK OUT ON THEIR OWN
teach.b: She doesn't have to wish: oh, may my chicks break out of their shells with their claws and beaks. If she keeps sitting, they will break out safely, on their own.
So it is, Ananda says, with someone who keeps these qualities warm. They're able to break through. The hen doesn't push the chicks or crack the shells for them.
She doesn't lie awake worrying about hatching.
Her whole job is to stay on the eggs. Breaking out is the eggs' business. The same picture appears in another discourse, where the Buddha himself uses it.
And when Ananda finishes, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Ananda, good. You've taught the disciple in training well. You can't force the breakthrough.
You can keep the practice warm, day after day, and trust what warmth does.

how: Some Buddhist teachers use the hen simile to encourage steady, patient daily practice without straining for results; in MN 53 a senior disciple teaches while the Buddha rests and listens.

o: the monk who taught the picture of the hen
the Buddha's father, king of the Sakyans
the noble who built the new hall

games.q: the new hall in Kapilavatthu — tap the pairs.
p: lies down when his back aches
keeps her eggs warm, doesn't force them

s: the hen must wish hard for her chicks to hatch
she doesn't need to wish; if she keeps sitting properly, the chicks break out on their own.
the Buddha let Ananda teach while he rested his back
he lay down mindfully and listened, then praised Ananda's teaching.
the hen cracks the shells to help the chicks
the chicks break out with their own claws and beaks; her job is to keep them warm.

games.q: you're a hen sitting on ten eggs. days pass and nothing happens. what do you do?
o: peck the shells open to speed things up.
give up and find better eggs.
games.why: Ananda's hen keeps sitting. without wishing or forcing, the chicks break out safely when they're ready.

practice: Stay with the breath the way a hen stays on her eggs, holding warm whatever practice you keep on this path: this sit, a kindness, a precept, an honest word. Don't check for results or wish for hatching.
Each time the mind wanders off to ask whether this is working, come back and settle on the eggs again.

wordCard.voice: Ananda. The monk who taught that night, with a picture of practice: keep it warm and steady, and what's ready to break out will break out.

carryVoice: Your line: the hen on the eggs. Warmth, kept up, does its own work. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 53, Sekha Sutta (the disciple in training)
